chunks: Al-Husayn narrated from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from Ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who takes vinegar (khamr) and turns it into vinegar (khall). He said: There is no harm in it, provided he does not put into it that which causes it to turn back (to wine). The ruling in it is also what we mentioned in the first report, equally.

key_terms.الْخَمْرَ: Wine (specifically grape wine, often considered najasah/impure in Shia fiqh)
key_terms.خَلًّا: Vinear (the product of fermentation, considered halal if properly converted)
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm in it (a legal phrase indicating permissibility)
key_terms.يُقَلِّبُهَا: To turn it back (revert it to its previous state, i.e., wine)

ai.seo_question: What is the condition for wine to become permissible vinegar in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) ruled that wine converted into vinegar is permissible provided no external agent is added to reverse the transformation, a principle rooted in the concept of *istihlak* (substantial change). This ruling, consistent with earlier narrations, highlights the Shia juristic distinction between mere qualitative change and the addition of substances that alter the essence, ensuring the intoxicant's nature is fully eradicated.
